population.note: FICTIONAL. ~18.1% of ~262M adults ≈ 47.4M currently on an incretin for any reason. Age check: 52M×9% + 86M×18% + 63M×29% + 60M×15% ≈ 4.7+15.5+18.3+9.0 = 47.5M ≈ 18.2%. Who pays (approx.): commercial insurance 16.5M (mostly diabetes/cardiac codes), Medicare 9.1M (≈7.0M Part D diabetes/CVD + 2.1M Bridge obesity), Medicaid 4.0M (≈1.2M obesity in the 14 participating states), cash-pay 14.0M (TrumpRx, LillyDirect, NovoCare, oral starter doses), unapproved imports/gray ≈4.0M; total ≈47.6M. Cycling arithmetic: ever 25 − current 18.1 = 6.9% of adults used and are off now; ≈5.5% of adults are current users who have stopped at least once and restarted, plus ≈1.5% are off now after a prior restart → (5.5+1.5)/25 = 28% of ever-users have cycled. Stopped-ever ≈ 6.9+5.5 = 12.4% of adults, of whom 7.0/12.4 ≈ 56% restarted at least once — a multi-year cumulative figure consistent with 36–47% restarting within a year. The high current/ever ratio (72%) versus ~1/3 one-year persistence reflects survey under-recall of brief trials and the much higher persistence of diabetes users; the gap is flagged, not resolved. Off-drug population: ~18M adults have used and stopped; the bottom third is lower than 2026 trend would predict because employer retreat removed coverage for obesity-only users. Pediatric: ~0.9% of under-18s, overwhelmingly adolescents 12+; under-12 starts fell after state limits; upper-income skew persists.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge extended through Dec 2028 at unchanged $245/month to Medicare, $50 copay; ≈2.1M obesity-only beneficiaries enrolled → 2.1M × $245 × 12 ≈ $6.2B/yr federal. Medicaid: 14 states opted in at $245; ≈1.2M obesity enrollees → 1.2M × $245 × 12 ≈ $3.5B/yr (federal+state). Retatrutide excluded from Bridge pending negotiation. Diabetes and established-CVD indications covered under standard Part D and Medicaid.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India generics $8–48/month and still falling; Canada generic semaglutide ~CAD 85–115/month; Brazil, Mexico, Turkey, South Africa with local generics; generic semaglutide available in ~170 countries. US brand exclusivity unchanged to ~2031–32.
access.note: Price path stalled: the planned TrumpRx step-down from ~$349 to $245 for injectables was shelved in late 2027; injectables and maintenance-dose orals sit at $299–499 cash; oral starter doses remain $149. Retatrutide list $1,449, LillyDirect cash $999, supply-allocated. Employer coverage for weight management fell 60%→44% (Business Group on Health, fictional 2028 survey); most remaining plans require BMI≥35 or a comorbidity and exclude retatrutide. Coverage concentrates on diabetes and cardiac codes, producing a two-tier system: coded patients pay $25–75 copays, obesity-only patients pay $300+ cash. With 503B compounding closed, the gray market moved to mailed Canadian and Indian generic semaglutide (FDA personal-importation discretion rarely enforced for 90-day supplies) and research-peptide retatrutide sold 'not for human use'; ≈4M adults rely on such sources.

drugs.pipeline_note: Retatrutide BLA filed Feb 2027, approved Apr 2028 (≈14 months; no voucher used) for obesity at ~28% mean loss; dysesthesia (known from phase 3) labelled; launch supply-constrained, ≈400k patients by Dec 2028. safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None as a safety matter; FDA untitled letters target implied claims in 'calm/focus' marketing.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households ~30% of US households; snack and confectionery volumes down mid-single digits cumulatively; brands sell smaller packs at higher unit price; protein and fibre callouts dominant; the aesthetic inversion gives a niche lift to 'unapologetic' indulgent and high-protein 'eat to build' products aimed at the unmedicated young.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes declining for a fourth year; heavy-drinker cohort shrinking on-drug and via off-label addiction prescribing; premium small-serve and non-alcoholic lines expanding but not offsetting.

restaurants.state: Traffic flat; smaller plates and 'tasting' formats standard; in Manhattan and LA a counter-trend of large-format 'appetite' menus marketed to the unmedicated.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists consolidating; mainstream brands add athletic-cut and 'build' sizing as muscle becomes the status silhouette; regain among coverage-losers creates erratic size demand.

fitness.state: Strength gyms and coaching the fastest-growing segment; 'natty' (unmedicated) branding spreads from bodybuilding to boutique gyms; GLP-1 companion programmes persist for the medicated.

insurance.state: Employer coverage for weight management 44%; exclusions of retatrutide near-universal; pharmacy trend moderating as obesity-only claims shift to cash; diabetes/CVD coding scrutiny rising.

pharma.state: Lilly dominant with tirzepatide and retatrutide; Novo defending with oral Wegovy and CagriSema; US prices held by capacity limits and political deals; ex-US revenue pressured by generics.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thinness reads as purchased and generic; visible muscle and a hearty appetite read as scarce and earned. 'Natty' is a compliment outside gyms.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Inverted at the top: affluent 22–40-year-olds in Brooklyn, Austin and LA signal status by being unmedicated and muscular, while middle-aged and middle-income Americans pay $300+ cash to stay thin; the bottom third, losing coverage, is the most likely to regain.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: In GLP-1 households meals are small and scheduled; among the status young, eating large in public is a performance of vitality. Families split: medicated parents, unmedicated teenagers.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating apps added an optional 'natty' profile badge in 2028; disclosing a drug became a sorting variable; anecdotes of muted desire persist and are now partly reframed as 'calm'.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has become a class marker: suppressing it is ordinary and paid for; having and indulging it is the new display of health.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Still unmeasured clinically. Telehealth 'Quiet'-style programmes report ~600k members (fits within the ≈14M cash-pay users and ≈4M gray-market users), many without obesity, on low-dose oral semaglutide or Foundayo off-label.
interior_life.framing: Feature: 'freedom from craving', calm, focus — sold as wellness programmes with coaching, legally framed to avoid drug claims; critics call it pacification, users call it quiet.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Adopted in finance, sales and software as an anti-distraction tool; some managers report steadier output, others less ambition and fewer stretch goals. No controlled data.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Musicians and comedians publicly split; a genre of 'off-dose' work made after stopping; hobby spending shifts from bars and gaming to structured activities; maximal-flavour foods and loud sensation media sell to users chasing reward.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples where one partner is 'quiet' report fewer fights and less desire in the same breath; therapists name 'dose mismatch' as a presenting issue.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: An issue rather than a behaviour change: wellness-sceptic conservatives and left critics both attack 'calm marketing' as sedation for profit; no measured effect on turnout.

state.regulatory_posture: Restrictive at the edges, pro-access at the core: fast reviews for obesity drugs continue, while advertising, paediatric use and telehealth initiation are curbed.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Medicare Bridge extended through 2028 at $245/$50; Medicaid opt-in in 14 states; cash price step-down abandoned.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Prior authorisation and coding audits for diabetes/CVD claims; 19 states require in-person initiation for BMI<27; no adherence monitoring.
state.workforce_or_military: None formal; DoD continues to exclude obesity-only use for active duty, unchanged.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: US–India price gap (~$349 vs ~$15) is a campaign talking point; personal imports tolerated; manufacturers cite capacity and tariffs to hold US prices.

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now: Inside the Year America Started Paying to Stay Hungry, and Bragging About Being Hungry
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 nearly one American adult in five takes an incretin drug, and the shock is how ordinary it has become. About 47 million adults are on one. Another 18 million tried and stopped, and more than a quarter of everyone who has ever used one has quit and started again at least once. The drugs did not get cheaper. The step-down in cash prices promised in 2025 was quietly dropped in late 2027, when Lilly and Novo pointed to factories busy with new launches. A weekly pen or a maintenance-dose pill now costs $299 to $499 a month without insurance. The $149 starter pills are still there to get people going. Wegovy's $1,349 list price, which nobody pays, hasn't changed either.

What changed is who pays. Employers kept walking away. Fewer than half now cover weight loss, and those that do cover mostly diabetes and heart patients. The result is two tiers. With a diabetes or cardiac code you pay a $40 copay. With obesity alone you pay cash, and 14 million people do, putting roughly fifty billion dollars a year on household credit cards. Medicare's Bridge pilot, still paying $245 with a $50 copay, was extended one year and covers about two million beneficiaries. Fourteen state Medicaid programmes joined. The rest are waiting on budgets. Below that sits a mail-order economy of Canadian and Indian generic semaglutide, which costs a fifteenth of the US price in Delhi. Customs mostly lets small personal orders through.

The new drug of the year is retatrutide. Approved in April, it delivers weight loss close to surgery from a weekly pen. It costs $999 cash, supply is rationed, and almost no insurer covers it. The people who get it are mostly the people who already had everything else.

Washington tightened the edges and left the core alone. Compounding is over. Weight-drug ads are gone from television and influencer feeds. Eleven states now require a specialist before anyone under sixteen starts, and bar under-twelves outside trials. Nineteen states require an in-person visit to start anyone who isn't overweight. No new indications arrived, and no new safety signal. The old ledger stands: nausea, gallbladder, muscle loss, the unresolved eye question, regain after stopping, and nothing known about decades of on-and-off use.

Into the gap stepped telehealth. Barred from selling weight loss loudly, the platforms sell quiet. Their 'craving freedom' memberships, built on low-dose pills, promise calm, focus and an end to the 2 a.m. scroll. About 600,000 people have signed up, many of them not overweight at all. The FDA sends letters about the wording and the programmes change their names. Salespeople and software engineers swap dosing tips the way an earlier generation swapped notes on Adderall. Therapists now see couples for 'dose mismatch'.

The culture has turned over. When thinness costs $349 a month and is everywhere, it stops meaning much. Among affluent twenty- and thirty-somethings in Brooklyn, Austin and Los Angeles, the prized body is muscled and visibly unmedicated, and so is the appetite that goes with it. 'Natty' has left the bodybuilding forums and become a dating-app badge. Restaurants in lower Manhattan serve big-format 'appetite' menus to people who want to be seen finishing a plate. Their parents eat small, scheduled meals and pay cash to keep doing it.

Snack volumes keep slipping and spirits fall for a fourth year. Plus-size retail keeps consolidating, and strength gyms can't build fast enough. None of this looks like a crisis. It looks like a country sorting itself: by insurance code, by who can afford to stay on, and by who can afford to be seen without it.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Alvarado wakes at 5:40 in Mesa and takes the pill before coffee, because the instructions say to. Foundayo, $329 this month on the LillyDirect card. Last year her dental group's plan paid. Then the letter came: weight management covered only with a qualifying diagnosis. Her A1c is fine, so she pays.

At the practice, Dr. Kessler eats a bagel with both halves and talks about his deadlift. Denise scales and polishes and doesn't think about lunch until two, and then only because the clock says so. Half a turkey wrap. The other half goes back in the bag for tomorrow.

Her sister texts a photo of a box from Vancouver: generic, ninety days, $260 total. You should, it says. Denise types something and deletes it.

In the car she listens to a podcast host selling a craving-freedom membership: calm, clarity, no more noise. She knows the noise. She doesn't miss it. Sometimes she misses the song she used to sing on this stretch of the 60, but she can't remember which one.

Her daughter Marisol, seventeen, is at the kitchen counter eating cereal out of a mixing bowl after practice, forearms veined. The app on her phone says natty under her name.

'You want some?' Marisol says. She's not being mean. That's the strange part.

Denise opens the fridge and stands in the cold light. She does the math again: $329, the car payment, Marisol's club fees. She closes the door. She sets out tomorrow's pill beside the coffee maker, where she'll see it.

least_plausible_claims.why: Ever-use sits at the very top of the envelope (25.1), a +10pp jump against a +7.1pp current-use rise. The 72% current/ever ratio contradicts the ~1/3 one-year persistence, and the note itself says the gap is flagged, not resolved. This is a magnitude/reconciliation strain.

least_plausible_claims.quote: putting roughly fifty billion dollars a year on household credit cards
least_plausible_claims.why: 14M cash-pay users at $299–499/month (many on $149 starters) comes to roughly $50–84B only if all pay full price. The figure appears only in prose, with no arithmetic in the world state, and the prose also says 14 million cash-pay people pay obesity-only cash, which conflicts with the commercial and gray splits. Magnitude is shaky and unshown.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Telehealth 'Quiet'-style programmes report ~600k members (fits within the ≈14M cash-pay users and ≈4M gray-market users)
least_plausible_claims.why: A 600k programme that took off within months of a Feb 2028 launch, and spread to finance, sales and software as a norm, is a fast jump from the 2026 'niche side effect'. Pairing it with a rapid in-person initiation rollout in 19 states makes the uptake weakly supported by a mechanism.

rationale.badness: Inequality is the main driver. A two-tier system by diagnosis code splits coded patients paying $25–75 from obesity-only patients paying $300+ cash, and the bottom third regains weight after losing coverage. Autonomy and epistemic scores reflect marketed calm/craving-freedom programmes, with reward blunting unmeasured and regulators policing words rather than the drug, plus gray-market 'research' retatrutide of unknown purity. Cohesion suffers from 'dose mismatch' in couples and medicated parents beside unmedicated teenagers, but the world is a harder society rather than a collapsed one.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Every driver is visibly realised in fields and dated events: stalled price, employer retreat to 44%, retatrutide approved Apr 2028, aesthetic inversion with the 'natty' badge, restrictions in 2027, and marketed-feature personality. Retatrutide approval about 14 months after the Feb 2027 filing fits the approval rule. Minor tension: CagriSema approval in Mar 2027 sits only about 15 months after a Dec 2025 filing, which is allowed. mechanism: Employer retreat to price-stalled cash tiers to regain among coverage-losers is a well-shown chain. The speed of the telehealth 'quiet' boom and the elite aesthetic inversion becoming a dating-app badge by 2028 are thinly supported, and the mention of 'Bridge extended' while price stalls is just asserted. magnitude: Current use at 18.1% and ever-use at 25 sit inside the envelope, but ever-use is pinned at the upper edge with a 72% current/ever ratio that the note admits is unresolved. The payer split sums to about 47.6M, and Medicare's 2.1M and Medicaid's 1.2M figures multiply correctly ($6.2B and $3.5B). The pediatric 0.9% and the prose's $50B cash claim are weakly reconciled, and 'about 18M stopped' versus 6.9% of 262M (≈18.1M) is fine.
rationale.generativity: The day-in-the-life with Denise, her sister's Vancouver box, and Marisol's cereal bowl and 'natty' badge carries a lot of texture, and it shows rather than explains. The world implies many scenes, including dose-mismatch therapy, unmedicated-only gym classes, 'appetite' menus and import parcels, so it supports a lot of film.

least_plausible_claims.why: Parent says BLA planned ~Q1 2027, so the 12-month rule is met. But the approval is stated flatly with no review mechanism, and a ~28% obesity label from a trial with 11.3% AE discontinuation is asserted. This is a mild magnitude and mechanism stretch.

least_plausible_claims.quote: CagriSema approved Mar 2027 after review, commercially weak given REDEFINE-4.
least_plausible_claims.why: CagriSema failed non-inferiority against tirzepatide, and the 2027 approval is asserted without a mechanism. It is permitted by the envelope, since it was under review at the start, so this is a minor mechanism flaw.

least_plausible_claims.quote: cash-pay 14.0M (TrumpRx, LillyDirect, NovoCare, oral starter doses)
least_plausible_claims.why: 14M cash payers at $299–499 a month, with cash prices rising for obesity-only users, sits oddly with employer retreat. The prose then converts this to 'roughly fifty billion dollars a year', which does not appear in the world and exceeds 14M × $300–$500 × 12 only if every user pays the top of that range. It also conflicts with the claim that 4M are on cheap imports.

rationale.badness: The two-tier system (coded patients on $25–75 copays versus obesity-only users on $300+ cash), regain concentrated in the bottom third, and about 4M adults on unverified imports and research peptides drive inequality and public health.
